answers.java_tx_design: Six years on our exchange's settlement ledger. Trade matching wrote the fill and debited/credited both accounts in one transaction that also called a risk-check service. Risk checks under load took up to 400ms, holding locks on hot accounts. I split it: write the fill and balance change fast, run risk checks async against a snapshot, flag for reversal if they fail after the fact. Lock contention on our top-10 trading pairs dropped by about 80%.
answers.java_ops: Connection pool starvation during a volatility spike — BTC dropped 8% in ten minutes, trade volume tripled. Pool capped at 40, requests queued past 2 seconds. I raised it to 100 after load-testing against Postgres headroom, and found a query doing a full scan on the trade-history table under that load. Added the missing index. Queue time during the next comparable spike stayed under 50ms.
answers.rust_readiness: No production Rust, but I've built two real side projects: a CLI that reconciles our exchange's public trade feed against my own paper-trading ledger, and a small websocket client for market data. Both taught me real lessons about ownership and async. No production plan yet, but I'd start narrow — a stateless dedup or rate-limit service — and measure before anything core moves.
answers.rust_boundary: I'd start with something stateless and latency-bound, not the ledger write itself. Interface as narrow as possible — one call in, one response out — so Java stays the source of truth during the transition. Watch p99 latency, memory, and error rate before and after, run it in shadow against the existing path on real traffic for a couple weeks before cutting over for real.
answers.money_correctness: Trade settlement uses an idempotency key from exchange match ID plus account ID, unique-constrained in Postgres. It broke once: a matching-engine retry after a network blip sent the same fill twice with different internal request IDs, since our key didn't account for that. 38 accounts got double-settled, about $94,000 in overstated balances. Caught in 12 minutes by our balance-vs-hot-wallet reconciliation job. Fixed with reversing entries, and widened the key to include match ID alone, not request ID.
answers.incident_response: That double-settlement is the clearest one. Reconciliation flagged it 12 minutes after the retry storm. I traced the cause — request ID leaking into the idempotency key — within about 15 minutes of the alert. Told my lead and risk as soon as I had the account list, not after the fix. Reversing entries posted for all 38 accounts within 40 minutes. Postmortem fix: idempotency key redesign plus an alert on match-ID retry rate itself.
answers.process_skipping: During that incident I shipped the key-redesign fix without our second reviewer — balances were actively wrong and every minute mattered. Posted the change and the skip in our incident channel before deploying, opened a real PR right after. Outside a live incident with real money moving wrong, I don't skip review. Confidence in a change isn't the same as someone else actually looking at it.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: Caught my own bug once — a caching change that served balances up to 60 seconds stale after a trade. Noticed it myself in a dashboard about an hour in, rolled it back, told the team the same day with the exact window it was live. On-call four years, one week in five. Mentored one engineer through their first six months on our reconciliation tooling.
answers.evidence_decision: Disagreed with a teammate who wanted a distributed lock around every settlement write. Pulled contention data showing the race window was under 5ms and rare. Proposed optimistic locking instead, showed the numbers, team agreed. Separately, the team chose synchronous settlement over my preferred async design for a launch deadline. I built it their way and didn't revisit it myself until the load numbers I'd predicted actually showed up months later.
answers.own_contribution: In the transaction-split I described, the redesign and the async risk-check path were mine. A teammate built the reversal-flagging UI for risk to review flagged trades — that wasn't something I touched. On the idempotency-key fix from the incident, that one was entirely mine, fix and postmortem both; the team's role there was reviewing it after the fact.
answers.java_recovery: A deploy window left about 90 trades with settlement status stuck at 'pending' though the fill had actually posted. Scoped it with a query for pending records older than our normal window, cross-checked against the matching engine's own fill log. Fixed with new 'settled' records rather than editing the stuck rows. Verified against the matching engine data for the whole window before closing it.
answers.java_perf_change: Balance-read endpoint sat at 220ms p99, mostly from joining the full trade-history table on every read. Added a maintained running-balance column updated transactionally on write. Got reads to about 25ms p99. First attempt used a nightly recompute batch instead — simpler, but let balances go stale for up to a day in edge cases. Caught it in testing, switched to updating on write.
answers.rust_hands_on: The reconciliation CLI: I had a shared HashMap I wanted multiple async tasks reading, reached for Rc<RefCell<>> out of habit, compiler rejected it — not Send. Switched to Arc<RwLock<>>. Then found I was holding the write lock across an await point during refresh, blocking readers longer than expected. Fixed by building the new data outside the lock and only locking for the final swap.
answers.rust_when_not: Wouldn't move the core matching-engine logic — changes every sprint with new order types, and nobody on the team has deep Rust experience yet. Held back an urge to rewrite the whole reconciliation pipeline after the CLI project went well. Measured what was actually slow first — one comparison step, not the whole pipeline — and scoped a real proposal down to that instead of pitching the rewrite.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: Daily settlement total was off from our hot-wallet balance by $3,100 across 22 accounts, flagged by the recon job's variance alert same afternoon. Cause: a rounding step for one trading pair rounded before a fee deduction instead of after, off by fractions of a cent per trade, additive over volume. Fixed with adjusting entries per account, corrected the rounding order. Took about two hours, most of it ruling out duplicates first.
answers.prod_data_verification: Wanted to check the reconciliation job's dedup logic against real trading patterns before trusting it. Built a shadow consumer reading the same fill stream read-only, comparing its decisions against production without writing anything. Two-week dry run surfaced four disagreements, all from a retry pattern I hadn't accounted for, fixed before it touched a real balance. Shadow mode first, always, before a new path gets to decide anything real.
